author: Declaration Desk
title: Christine Lagarde to leave the European Central Bank in February, months before her term ends
dek: The ECB president will step down on February 7, 2027, giving EU leaders time to name a successor before France votes in April. The bank held its deposit rate at 2.5%.
body:
Christine Lagarde will step down as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) on February 7, 2027, about nine months before her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027, she announced on Thursday, October 29.

Lagarde, 70, made the announcement in a short video on social media, saying she would leave "with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future", Reuters and AFP reported. She informed the bank's Governing Council and European Council President António Costa shortly before the ECB announced its latest interest rate decision.

## The rate decision

On the same day the ECB kept its deposit rate unchanged at 2.5%, Reuters reported, after raising rates in June and September as energy prices pushed up inflation. It signalled that another increase was likely, possibly as soon as December. Money markets are pricing in about three more hikes by the end of 2027, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%.

Financial markets showed little reaction to Lagarde's announcement, Reuters reported. Analysts said the bank's policy was unlikely to change much whoever succeeded her.

## Why now

Lagarde gave no detailed reason. A source told Reuters she had resigned so that she could speak on political matters in France and globally; she has said she will not run for the French presidency. Media reports have linked her to a senior role at the World Economic Forum, which declined to comment.

The timing is significant. France holds a presidential election in April 2027, and polls suggest the far-right Marine Le Pen is the front-runner. Leaving in February allows the current European Council, including outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron, to choose her successor before the vote. Macron said the transition should be prepared "in an orderly and balanced manner" with European partners.

Not everyone welcomed it. Markus Ferber, a German member of the European Parliament from the centre-right EPP group, warned that a departure timed around national elections could damage trust in the institution. Jean-Philippe Tanguy, an economist who works on Le Pen's programme, called it an insult. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Lagarde had led the bank with great aplomb in difficult times.

## What happens next

Costa said the process to choose a successor would begin at once, with a view to a timely decision by EU leaders of euro-area countries; the European Parliament is consulted on the nomination. The former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and the former Spanish central bank governor Pablo Hernández de Cos are widely seen as front-runners, Reuters reported. The choice is likely to be part of a wider reshuffle at the ECB, where board member Isabel Schnabel leaves in early January and chief economist Philip Lane in May.

Lagarde, a former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, has led the ECB since November 2019. According to Investing.com, the only earlier ECB president not to complete a full term was Wim Duisenberg, whose early exit was agreed in advance in 1998.

For India, the ECB's direction matters through its effect on global interest rates, the euro-rupee exchange rate and capital flows into emerging markets; the US Federal Reserve held its rates earlier this week.
